## How to Choose a CMS for a School Website

To choose a CMS for a school website, prioritise ease of content updates, approval workflows, mobile performance, security, accessibility and support over the number of features listed in a demo. The right content management system should allow authorised school staff to publish accurate information without depending on a developer for every notice, while giving the school control over student privacy, admissions content and costs.

A school website is not only a digital brochure. It may be used by parents checking admission details, existing families looking for circulars, students downloading timetables, teachers accessing resources, job applicants reviewing vacancies and local visitors verifying the school’s contact information.

That makes CMS selection a practical operational decision. A system that looks attractive but is difficult to update can quickly lead to outdated fee information, missed notices and broken links. A simpler CMS with clear permissions and dependable support may be a better fit.

## 1. Understand What the School Website Needs to Do

Before comparing WordPress, Drupal, website builders or a custom CMS, list the website’s regular jobs. The right system depends on the school’s communication process, not just its design preferences.

### Common school website requirements

Most schools need some combination of the following:

- Home page with announcements and important links
- About the school, leadership and governing body information
- Academic programmes, curriculum and facilities
- Admissions process, eligibility and required documents
- Fee-related guidance, without exposing confidential student information
- Notices, circulars, examination schedules and holiday lists
- Events calendar and photo galleries
- Faculty and staff information
- Careers or recruitment pages
- Contact forms, enquiry forms and location details
- Downloadable PDFs such as forms, prospectuses and annual reports
- News, achievements and activity updates
- Parent or student login, if required
- Integration with a school management or ERP platform

Some schools also need separate sections for pre-primary, primary, secondary and senior secondary education. Others operate multiple campuses and require one website with location-specific pages.

The CMS should support these needs without forcing staff to create complicated workarounds. For example, if the school publishes weekly circulars, uploading a PDF should be straightforward. If notices must be removed or archived after a defined period, the system should support that process clearly.

### Separate public content from private functions

A public school website and a parent portal are not necessarily the same product.

The public website may contain admission dates, campus information and general notices. A parent portal may contain attendance, report cards, fee receipts or personal communications. These private functions require stronger access controls and may be better handled by an existing school ERP rather than added to the website CMS.

Combining everything into one system can increase complexity and security responsibility. In many cases, the better approach is a public content management system connected to a separate school management platform through links or an integration.

### Identify the people who will use the CMS

The person who designs the website may not be the person who updates it. In a school, content may be managed by an administrator, principal’s office, admissions team, communications staff or a teacher given the responsibility as an additional duty.

Ask:

- Who will draft content?
- Who will approve it?
- Who will upload documents?
- Who can publish immediately?
- Who should only be able to edit certain pages?
- What happens when the responsible staff member leaves?
- Is there a backup person trained to use the system?

These questions help you evaluate permissions and workflows before selecting a platform.

## 2. Compare the Main CMS Options

There is no single best CMS for every school. The practical choice usually falls into one of three categories: a hosted website builder, a self-hosted open-source CMS or a custom-built content management system.

| CMS option | Suitable for | Main strengths | Main limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hosted website builder | Smaller schools with simple content needs | Easier hosting, basic maintenance handled by provider, quick setup | Limited flexibility, platform dependency, variable support and export options |
| Self-hosted open-source CMS | Schools needing flexibility and a broad ecosystem | Many themes and plugins, strong customisation, easier access to developers | Requires hosting, updates, security management and maintenance |
| Managed open-source CMS | Schools wanting flexibility with technical support | Open-source features with a support arrangement | Ongoing service dependency and recurring maintenance cost |
| Custom CMS | Institutions with unusual workflows or complex integrations | Tailored permissions, design and integrations | Higher development responsibility, testing and long-term maintenance |
| School ERP with website module | Schools already using an integrated school platform | Potential connection with admissions, notices and parent data | Website design and content features may be limited |

### Hosted website builders

Hosted platforms generally include hosting, a visual editor and basic content functions. They may work for a small school that needs a few pages, contact details, occasional updates and a gallery.

Their appeal is simplicity. However, schools should check whether the platform supports the required Indian payment options, custom domains, SEO controls, backups, role-based access and data export. Some platforms make it difficult to move the website later.

A hosted builder can be appropriate when the school has limited technical support and does not expect complex integration. It may be less suitable when several departments need structured publishing workflows or when the website will grow significantly.

### Open-source CMS platforms

An open-source CMS such as WordPress can offer a wide range of themes, plugins and developer support. It is commonly considered when a school needs a content-heavy website with regular notices, event pages, downloadable documents and custom forms.

The software itself may be available without a licence fee, but the website still requires domain registration, hosting, development, security configuration, backups, updates and ongoing maintenance. “Free CMS” does not mean “free website”.

Open-source systems require disciplined administration. Plugins should be selected carefully, kept updated and removed when no longer required. A school should also know who is responsible for restoring the website if an update causes a problem.

### Custom CMS development

A custom CMS may make sense if the school has specific workflows that existing systems cannot support. Examples could include multiple campuses with different editorial teams, complex approval stages or an unusual integration with an internal platform.

Custom software is not automatically better. It creates a long-term responsibility for documentation, security updates, bug fixes, hosting and developer availability. Before approving it, the school should ask whether the special requirements are genuinely important enough to justify that responsibility.

## 3. Evaluate Content Management and Approval Workflows

Content management is the core reason for choosing a CMS. A good school website should make common tasks predictable for non-technical users.

### Check the editing experience

Ask for a demonstration using actual school tasks rather than generic sample text. Request that the provider show how to:

- Add a new announcement
- Set a publication and expiry date
- Upload a PDF
- Replace an outdated document
- Add a page to the main menu
- Publish an event
- Update a phone number
- Add an image with alternative text
- Remove an old notice
- Restore an earlier version of a page

A system may look easy when shown by an experienced developer but become confusing for a staff member using it occasionally. The school should test the dashboard with people who will actually manage the content.

### Look for roles and permissions

At minimum, a school may need separate roles for contributors, editors and administrators.

For example:

- A teacher can draft an event update.
- The communications coordinator can review wording and images.
- The principal’s office can approve and publish it.
- A technical administrator can manage users, backups and settings.

This reduces the risk of an unreviewed notice being published. It also prevents every user from having access to sensitive configuration settings.

Check whether the CMS supports:

- Multiple users with individual logins
- Strong password policies
- Two-factor authentication where available
- Draft and review status
- Scheduled publishing
- Revision history
- Approval workflows
- User activity logs
- Access restrictions by section or department

Individual accounts are preferable to one shared password. When staff change roles, their access should be removed or updated promptly.

### Plan for document management

School websites often become repositories of PDFs. Over time, files may include duplicate versions, unclear names and outdated information.

The CMS should make it easy to:

- Use descriptive file names
- Replace a document without creating confusion
- Identify where a PDF is linked
- Organise files by academic year or content type
- Remove old documents from public access
- Keep important documents available in an accessible format

A file named `circular-final-new2.pdf` is difficult to manage. A more useful naming convention might include the document type and date, provided the school applies it consistently.

## 4. Assess Design, Mobile Usability and Accessibility

Parents and students may access a school website from mobile phones, often through a messaging app link. The website should therefore be designed for small screens first, not treated as a desktop page reduced to fit a phone.

### Test common mobile actions

Check whether users can quickly:

- Read an urgent notice
- Open a PDF
- Call the school
- Find the address and directions
- Submit an enquiry
- View admission information
- Navigate between academic sections
- Read the page without horizontal scrolling

Buttons should be large enough to tap, menus should be understandable and important information should not be buried beneath decorative elements.

Page speed also matters. Large images, autoplay videos, excessive sliders and poorly configured plugins can make a school website slow on mobile networks. The CMS should support image compression, caching and sensible media management.

### Include accessibility from the beginning

Accessibility helps users with disabilities and improves usability for everyone. It should not be added only after the website is built.

Useful requirements include:

- Proper heading structure
- Keyboard-friendly navigation
- Sufficient colour contrast
- Alternative text for meaningful images
- Captions or transcripts for important video content
- Labels for forms
- Clear link text
- Visible focus states
- Avoidance of text embedded only inside images
- Compatibility with commonly used assistive technologies

Schools should also publish documents in formats that are reasonably accessible. A scanned image of a notice may be difficult for screen readers and inconvenient for search. Where practical, provide selectable text and a web page summary.

India’s Rights of Persons with Disabilities framework and public-sector accessibility expectations make accessibility a meaningful consideration for education websites. Even where a specific requirement does not directly apply to a private school, inclusive design is a sensible standard.

## 5. Check Security, Privacy and Compliance Responsibilities

A school website may handle personal information through admission forms, enquiry forms, staff applications, event registrations and newsletter subscriptions. This makes security and privacy part of CMS selection.

### Ask how data is protected

Before selecting a CMS or vendor, clarify:

- Where website and form data are hosted
- Who can access submissions
- How backups are taken and retained
- How quickly security updates are applied
- Whether malware monitoring is included
- How administrator accounts are protected
- What happens if the website is compromised
- How data is deleted when no longer required
- Whether access logs are available

The website should use HTTPS through a valid SSL certificate. Forms should collect only information that is necessary for the stated purpose. Sensitive student data should not be placed in public pages, filenames or image galleries without appropriate consent and controls.

### Consider the Digital Personal Data Protection framework

Schools should review their responsibilities under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act and applicable rules as they develop. The exact obligations can depend on the organisation, data collected, consent process and how children’s data is handled.

For online forms, provide clear information about why data is collected, how it will be used and how a person can contact the organisation about their data. Children’s information requires additional care. A public website should not expose student names, photographs or achievements without the school’s internal approval and appropriate permissions.

The CMS cannot solve governance problems by itself. The school should maintain a simple privacy policy, define who can access form submissions and establish a process for correcting or deleting information where appropriate.

### Be cautious with third-party plugins and scripts

Contact forms, analytics, chat tools, maps, video embeds and social media feeds may send information to external services. The school should know what each integration does and whether it is necessary.

Avoid installing plugins simply because they offer an attractive feature. Every additional plugin can introduce maintenance, compatibility and security concerns. Use reputable tools, keep them updated and remove unused components.

## 6. Consider SEO, Search and Communication Needs

A school website needs to be findable for searches such as the school’s name, location, admissions information and contact details. CMS selection affects whether staff can maintain the basics of search optimisation.

### Important SEO controls

The CMS should allow the school to manage:

- Page titles
- Meta descriptions
- Clean and readable URLs
- Heading structure
- Image alternative text
- Internal links
- XML sitemap
- Canonical URLs where needed
- Redirects when pages move
- Search engine indexing settings

These controls do not guarantee rankings. They simply help search engines understand the website and help the school avoid common technical problems.

Local information should be accurate and consistent. The school’s name, address, phone number, email address and campus details should match across the website and relevant local listings. If the school has more than one campus, each location should have a clear page rather than combining addresses in a confusing format.

### Make notices searchable and organised

A long list of PDF links is difficult for parents to use. Notices should ideally have:

- A clear title
- Publication date
- Category or audience
- Short summary
- Download link
- Archive or expiry method

A search function can help when the website contains several years of circulars. However, search quality depends on how content is structured. A CMS with categories, tags or custom content types may be more useful than a basic page editor.

### Connect the website to communication channels carefully

Indian schools commonly share website links through WhatsApp groups, email, SMS platforms and social media. The CMS should produce clean, stable page links that are easy to share.

Avoid treating WhatsApp as the permanent storage location for official information. A notice should ideally live on the school website, with the message linking to it. This gives parents a reliable reference and allows the school to update or archive content in one place.

## 7. Review Hosting, Support and Total Cost

The cost of a school website is not limited to design and development. The school should evaluate the complete ownership model over several years.

### Typical cost categories

Budget planning may include:

- Domain registration and renewal
- Hosting or platform subscription
- Website design and development
- CMS configuration
- Content migration
- Photography or media preparation
- SSL and security services
- Plugin or theme licences
- Maintenance and updates
- Backup and monitoring
- Support and training
- GST on applicable services
- Future changes and integrations

Market costs vary widely depending on the number of pages, design expectations, integrations, content volume, accessibility work and support arrangement. A small brochure-style website and a multi-campus platform with admissions integration should not be compared as if they are the same project.

The school should ask whether quoted work is a one-time build or includes ongoing maintenance. It should also clarify what counts as a minor content update, a new feature or a separate development task.

### Compare support arrangements

Support is particularly important when school staff are not technical users. Ask:

- Who will respond when the website is unavailable?
- Is support provided by email, phone or WhatsApp?
- Are emergency fixes handled separately?
- Is content uploading included?
- How are software updates tested?
- Is staff training included?
- Will the school receive documentation?
- What happens if the agency stops supporting the CMS?

Do not select a platform solely because it is familiar to the developer. The school should have reasonable access to its domain, hosting, CMS administrator account, website files and database, subject to the agreed security arrangement.

### Plan for staff turnover

School staff responsibilities can change frequently. A website should not depend on one person’s private email account or undocumented knowledge.

Maintain:

- A current administrator list
- Written publishing procedures
- Backup contact details
- Basic CMS training material
- A record of integrations and renewal dates
- A content calendar
- A process for handing over access

This is one of the most practical benefits of choosing a well-supported and widely understood CMS.

## 8. Use a Structured CMS Selection Process

A short selection process can prevent an expensive mismatch.

### Step 1: Create a requirements list

Divide needs into three groups:

- Must have: essential for launch
- Should have: useful but not essential
- Could have: future improvements

For example, mobile responsiveness, notices and staff permissions may be essential. A virtual tour or advanced search may be a later addition.

### Step 2: Review real examples carefully

Look beyond visual design. Test the sites on a phone, open their menus, inspect forms and check how quickly important content can be found.

A good-looking homepage does not show whether the CMS is easy to manage. Ask the provider to demonstrate the administrative side using the school’s own sample content.

### Step 3: Ask for a written proposal

The proposal should describe:

- Scope of pages and features
- Content responsibilities
- CMS and hosting arrangement
- User roles
- Integrations
- Security and backup approach
- Training
- Support period
- Renewal charges
- Ownership and access
- GST treatment
- Exclusions and assumptions

Written clarity is more useful than verbal assurances.

### Step 4: Run a content management test

Give shortlisted providers a small test such as:

1. Create a notice for parents.
2. Schedule it for a future date.
3. Upload a PDF.
4. Add an image with alternative text.
5. Submit it for approval.
6. Replace the PDF.
7. Archive the notice.

The purpose is not to conduct a technical examination. It is to see whether the workflow is understandable to the school’s actual users.

### Step 5: Decide who owns the website

The school should retain practical control over its domain name, content and important accounts. If an agency manages hosting, the agreement should explain how access and migration work if the relationship ends.

Ownership should be discussed before development begins, not after a dispute arises.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Which CMS is best for a school website?

There is no universal answer. A hosted builder may suit a small school with simple content, while WordPress or another open-source CMS may be better for a school needing flexible pages, notices and integrations. The best choice is the one staff can operate securely and consistently within the school’s budget and support capacity.

### Is WordPress suitable for education websites?

WordPress can be suitable for school websites because it supports pages, posts, forms, media, user roles and many integrations. It requires proper hosting, updates, backups and plugin management. A school should not treat the installation as complete simply because the website is live.

### Should a school website include a parent login?

Only if there is a clear operational need and suitable security controls. If the school already uses an ERP for attendance, marks, fees or personal communications, linking to that system may be safer than duplicating private functions inside the public CMS.

### How often should school website content be updated?

There is no fixed schedule for every page. Admission details, contact information, calendars and notices should be reviewed regularly, while less-changing pages can be reviewed at least once each academic year. Each page should have an internal owner responsible for checking whether its information remains accurate.

### How much does a school CMS website cost in India?

The amount depends on design complexity, page count, content migration, integrations, hosting, maintenance, support and GST. A basic website and a multi-campus system have very different requirements. Govindani Infotech confirms its own project pricing with clients on WhatsApp after understanding the scope.

### Can a school change its CMS later?

It can, but migration may require moving pages, images, documents, forms, redirects and user data. Some hosted platforms make export difficult, so portability should be discussed before signing up. Keeping domain ownership and maintaining an organised content structure makes a future change easier.

## Where to Start

Begin by documenting the school’s audiences, regular content types, approval process and private-data requirements. Shortlist two or three CMS approaches, test each with real school tasks, and compare the complete cost of hosting, maintenance, training, support and GST rather than comparing only the initial development quote.

Before approving the project, confirm ownership of the domain and content, administrator access, backup responsibilities, privacy procedures and the process for updating the website after launch.
